papers.title: Integrating GWAS meta-analysis with human brain cell mapping implicates the amygdala and cortical inhibitory interneurons in tinnitus
papers.abstract: Purpose: Tinnitus is a common and heterogeneous condition whose genetic architecture remains poorly defined and whose definition varies across studies. We asked which common genetic variants are associated with tinnitus, to what extent genetic associations are shared across heterogeneous tinnitus definitions, and in which brain cell populations tinnitus heritability is concentrated. Methods: Genome-wide association meta-analysis of 19 independent population-based cohorts from Europe and the United States (hereby named EARGEN), comprising 961,085 adults of European ancestry (75,584 tinnitus cases and 885,501 controls). Tinnitus was defined by self-report in 17 cohorts and by diagnostic codes in two. Single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) based heritability and genetic correlations were estimated by linkage disequilibrium score regression, genes were mapped by gene-based association together with positional and expression quantitative trait locus mapping. Heritability enrichment was tested by stratified linkage disequilibrium score regression across 31 brain cell superclusters derived from post-mortem human brain donors, and across the 461 cell clusters that compose them. Enrichment was tested for replication in the Million Veteran Program (MVP) under a self-report definition (114,325 cases, 201,343 controls) and a diagnostic-code definition (77,601 cases, 310,953 controls). Results: Five independent loci reached genome-wide significance (p < 5 x 10-8) on chromosomes 2, 8, 12, 13 and 16, two of which (rs10877884 and rs2147632) have not been reported previously. SNP-based heritability was 0.0137 (SE = 0.0009) on the observed scale and 0.0535 (0.0036) on the liability scale. Genetic correlations were significant with hearing loss, anxiety disorder, major depressive disorder, chronic pain, and four further psychiatric, sleep and vestibular traits. Three superclusters showed a suggestive enrichment in the midbrain-derived inhibitory neurons, amygdala excitatory neurons, and medial ganglionic eminence interneurons at a false discovery rate (FRD) of 0.067, the two latter of which reached significance in the Million Veteran Program (MVP) under the diagnostic-code definition (0.030 and 0.006). At cluster resolution, the amygdala excitatory cluster was found significant (z = 4.82, false discovery rate = 3.3 x 10-4), whereas none of the ascending auditory relay cluster were found enriched (z [≤] 1.71, false discovery rate [≥] 0.21). Conclusion: Tinnitus-associated common variation concentrates in limbic and cortical neuronal populations rather than in the ascending auditory pathway. The predisposition to tinnitus therefore appears to be central and largely non-auditory in origin. The small number of genome-wide significant associations obtained despite a large sample emphasizes the need for more detailed and standardized phenotyping focusing on the tinnitus disorder.

papers.title: Nationwide Functional Profiling Enables Clinical Reclassification of KCNH2 Variants in the French LQT2 Population
papers.abstract: Background: The increasing use of genetic testing has identified thousands of KCNH2 variants associated with long QT syndrome type 2 (LQT2), yet most remain variants of uncertain significance (VUS). Translating functional abnormalities into clinically actionable evidence remains a major challenge. We established a nationwide functional genomics strategy to systematically characterize KCNH2 variants identified in the French LQT2 population and improve their clinical interpretation. Methods: We characterized 303 KCNH2 variants, including 201 VUS, using standardized high-throughput automated patch-clamp electrophysiology and complementary membrane trafficking assays. Nine electrophysiological parameters were integrated using MeTAL to predict variant-specific repolarization phenotypes under homozygous and heterozygous conditions. Modeled QTc values were compared with patient electrocardiographic data and variant-specific penetrance estimates. Functional evidence was calibrated against established benign and pathogenic variants using ClinGen-recommended categorical OddsPath and continuous likelihood-ratio approaches. Results: Multidimensional functional profiling revealed abnormalities not captured by current amplitude alone, identifying additional variants with clinically relevant repolarization defects. Among variants assessed under heterozygous conditions, MeTAL predictions showed 82.9% concordance with patient QTc phenotypes for ACMG class 5 variants, with apparent discordances partly consistent with incomplete penetrance. Continuous likelihood-ratio calibration demonstrated strong discrimination between established benign and pathogenic variants (AUC=0.936) and provided graded functional evidence for 76.1% of VUS. Integration of calibrated functional evidence into the ACMG/AMP framework enabled reclassification of 64 of 201 VUS (31.8%), including 7 as pathogenic, 46 as likely pathogenic, and 11 as likely benign. Conclusions: This nationwide study establishes a scalable framework integrating high-throughput electrophysiology, computational modeling, and clinical phenotyping to translate complex KCNH2 channel dysfunction into clinically interpretable evidence. The resulting reclassification of nearly one-third of VUS, together with the open-access HAMMER database, provides a resource to improve molecular diagnosis and risk assessment in LQT2.

papers.title: Cross-cohort validation of EEG biomarkers using a pre-registered three-criterion framework: a demonstration in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
papers.abstract: Background. Despite decades of EEG biomarker development for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), no candidate has progressed to clinical deployment, partly because cross-cohort validation is rare. We aimed to develop and demonstrate a pre-registered three-criterion screening framework to identify which candidate EEG features show the combined properties required for biomarker translation: cross-sectional discrimination, within-subject reliability, and cross-cohort effect consistency. Methods. We pre-registered a validation framework adapted from FDA-NIH BEST principles and applied it to 18 EEG features across three independent cohorts: EEGET-ALS (six ALS patients, 170 healthy controls; home recordings over 17 days), UCL/Penn State (eight ALS patients; clinic recordings over 1-2 months), and a healthy adult test-retest reference (60 participants, three sessions over one month). Features were required to meet three pre-registered criteria: (1) cross-sectional discrimination (Cohen's d > 0.5), (2) within-subject reliability (ICC(3,1) > 0.6 in both ALS cohorts independently), and (3) cross-cohort effect direction consistency. Cross-cohort permutation testing (1000 iterations) and subject-level bootstrap resampling (500 iterations) were applied to assess robustness. Results. Three features met all three pre-registered criteria: gamma power, theta power, and spectral entropy. Cross-cohort permutation testing showed that no permutation, out of 1000, produced any feature in the three-cohort reliability intersection (Monte Carlo p = 0.001). Bootstrap resampling indicated that the composition of the selected set was sensitive to sample composition (median count 1, 95% CI [0, 4]), with gamma power (67% inclusion), spectral entropy (43%), and theta power (32%) the most stable features at a relaxed reliability threshold (ICC > 0.5); at the primary pre-registered threshold (ICC > 0.6), the corresponding inclusion probabilities are lower (57%, 27%, and 19%, respectively). A principal methodological finding was that cross-cohort differences in feature reliability were large relative to the apparent disease-associated signal, most clearly demonstrated by relative beta power (ICC = 0.09 in a home-recorded cohort versus 0.93 in a clinic-recorded cohort); because recording protocol, hardware, setting, population, and preprocessing all differ jointly between cohorts in this dataset, this is evidence of cohort-associated variability that plausibly includes a protocol contribution, not a separately identified, isolated protocol effect. Conclusions. This study provides a pre-registered, multi-cohort EEG biomarker screening framework for ALS with explicit bootstrap-quantified uncertainty. Gamma power, spectral entropy, and theta power are identified as priority candidates for prospective validation. A recurring methodological observation is that protocol-related cohort differences appear to contribute more to cross-cohort variability than disease-related effects within this dataset; because protocol is confounded with cohort, equipment, and preprocessing, this pattern is descriptive rather than causal. The observation nonetheless has direct implications for the design of multi-site EEG biomarker studies in neural engineering.

papers.title: Sub-Threshold Stochastic Vibration Improves Fingertip Tactile Sensitivity in Stroke Survivors and Healthy Adults, with Source-Localized EEG Evidence for Cortical Network Reorganization in Healthy Adults
papers.abstract: Cutaneous sensation is vital for daily function and safety, yet it commonly declines with ageing and after neurological injury, with stroke survivors particularly affected. This study investigates whether sub-threshold stochastic (random) vibrations can enhance light-touch (cutaneous) sensation in healthy adults and stroke survivors and characterizes the associated changes in cortical functional connectivity (FC). Nineteen healthy participants and five stroke survivors took part. A custom device delivered sinusoidal and stochastic vibrations to the volar surface of the right middle fingertip. For each participant we first determined the detection threshold for stochastic vibration alone, then the threshold for a 30 Hz sinusoidal vibration, and then the threshold for that sinusoidal vibration combined with imperceptible stochastic noise fixed at 80% of the stochastic threshold; in ten healthy participants a super-threshold combination (120% of the stochastic threshold) was also tested. High-density (64-channel) electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded throughout for the healthy participants. Adding sub- threshold stochastic noise lowered the sinusoidal detection threshold in every participant tested and produced consistent reductions in all five stroke survivors; expressed as gains in sensitivity, individual improvements reached up to 19 times in healthy participants and up to 4 times in stroke survivors. Source- localized EEG showed that sub-threshold stochastic vibration significantly increased FC, most extensively in the alpha band, with prominent involvement of frontal regions (superior and rostral middle frontal cortices and anterior cingulate; cluster- based permutation p < 0.05), consistent with a noise-driven modulation of sensory and attentional networks. Super-threshold noise produced weaker, predominantly beta-band changes, in line with signal masking rather than resonance. These findings indicate that sub-threshold stochastic vibration lowers light-touch detection thresholds and reorganizes cortical connectivity in both healthy and stroke populations, and they support prioritizing cutaneous sensation in stochastic-resonance based neurorehabilitation for stroke survivors.

papers.title: Individualized systems-informed corrective exercise for adults meeting prespecified criteria for upper crossed syndrome: protocol for a randomized controlled trial
papers.abstract: Background: Heterogeneity in eligibility criteria, intervention content, and exercise-progression rules has limited the reproducibility of research on upper crossed syndrome. This trial will examine the added effect of a structured, individualized, staged corrective-exercise program on adults who meet prespecified criteria for this phenotype. Methods: In this parallel randomized controlled trial, 36 women and men aged 18-40 years with forward head and shoulder posture and increased thoracic kyphosis will be allocated 1:1, stratified by sex. Over 12 weeks, both groups will attend three sessions per week and receive stationary cycling, indication-based stretching and mobilization, and education on healthy movement habits. The intervention group will additionally receive a systems-informed program encompassing restoration of range of motion, muscle-activation retraining, correction of movement patterns, progressive load tolerance, and preparation for health-enhancing physical activity. The primary outcome is the baseline-adjusted week-12 between-group difference in a multivariate profile comprising the forward-head, forward-shoulder, and thoracic-kyphosis angles. Scapular-muscle electromyography, range of motion, and balance are secondary outcomes. The primary exploratory electroencephalographic outcome is change in central relative alpha power during quiet standing with eyes open. Posture, range of motion, and balance will be assessed at baseline, week 12, and four-week follow-up; electromyography and electroencephalography at baseline and week 12. The primary analysis will use MANCOVA adjusted for baseline and sex, with Pillai's trace; longitudinal analyses will use linear mixed models. Effect estimates and 95% confidence intervals will be reported. Conclusions: This study will test the added effect of a reproducible corrective-exercise framework beyond the shared active-control components. The four-week follow-up will not support inference about long-term prevention of recurrence. Ethics and trial registration: Ethics approval: IR.UI.REC.1404.053. Trial registration: IRCT20250921067305N1.

papers.title: Robust Feature Engineering Techniques for Designing Efficient Motor Imagery-Based Systems Using Multidomain Electroencephalography
papers.abstract: Motor imagery-based brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have potential applications in neurorehabilitation; however, the high dimensionality and complexity of electroencephalography (EEG) signals present challenges for accurate classification. This study aimed to improve the classification of motor and motor imagery activities using multidomain feature engineering and feature selection on the MILimbEEG dataset. Time-domain, frequency-domain, and wavelet-based features were extracted from 16-channel EEG signals, yielding 416 features. Maximum relevance minimum redundancy (MRMR) was then applied to select the four most informative and minimally redundant features. These features were used to train support vector machine (SVM), K-nearest neighbors (KNN), Naive Bayes, and decision tree classifiers, with performance evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation based on testing accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The Gaussian-kernel SVM achieved the highest testing accuracies of 92.50% for motor activities and 95.48% for motor imagery activities. For the highest-performing motor imagery classification, precision, recall, and F1-score were 86.97%, 88.33%, and 87.04%, respectively. These findings demonstrate that reducing 416 multidomain EEG features to four discriminative features using MRMR can maintain strong classification performance. The proposed feature-engineering framework may support the development of computationally efficient EEG-based BCI systems for neurorehabilitation applications.

papers.title: Automatic classification of seizure adequacy in electroconvulsive therapy: A proof-of-concept study
papers.abstract: Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is the most effective treatment of a range of severe mental dis-orders and is annually given to more than a million patients worldwide. Dosing of the electrical charge is critical for efficacy and side-effect burden; however, it is currently based on manual assessment of seizure quality and exhibits substantial clinical heterogeneity. Here, we collected 1,000 ECT session electroencephalograms (EEG) from 130 individual ECT patients and made an expert-level classification of the EEGs into actionable seizure quality categories (null-response [0], threshold [T], and adequate [A]). We then trained a range of machine learning algorithms on the raw EEG data to classify the EEGs into these categories and tested for classi-fication accuracy. The highest performing algorithm was able to classify the seizures with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curves of >0.9 for both the 0 vs. T and the T vs. A categories corresponding to excellent discrimination. In contrast, the accuracy of predicting seizure quality in subsequent treatments was only moderate. The addition of clinical variables to the models, such as demographics, anesthesia and anticonvulsant exposure, did not improve model performance. These results provide proof-of-concept of machine learning classification of seizure adequacy in ECT based on raw EEG data. The findings could pave the way for the de-velopment of more objective and personalized decision-support tools in ECT.

papers.title: Prevalence of Self-Reported Auditory Dysfunction Among Call Center Employees and Its Association with Shift Work Across Various Call Centers in Cairo, Egypt, March 2026
papers.abstract: Abstract Background The rapid, unregulated expansion of the call center industry in developing countries has increased occupational health risks for young adults, particularly with regard to auditory health. Prolonged exposure to acoustic trauma, long working hours, and the high intensity nature of call center work can negatively affect young adults at the start of their working lives and may contribute to permanent noise induced hearing loss (NIHL). This damage is often irreversible but preventable if identified at an early stage. This study aims to evaluate the burden of auditory impairment among call center employees in Egypt and to propose evidence based mitigation strategies. Methods A pilot cross sectional study was conducted among employees of various medical call centers over approximately three months (January to March 2026). Participants were recruited through voluntary (self selected) sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire on work history, and statistical analysis was performed to examine associations with work duration and intensity. Three semi structured, open ended interviews were conducted in March 2026 to explore the symptoms in greater depth. Results Forty six call center employees completed the questionnaire. The most frequently reported symptoms were mishearing words (82.6%), difficulty understanding speech in background noise (80.4%), needing others to repeat themselves (78.3%), and sensitivity to loud sounds (78.3%); 60.9% reported tinnitus. Higher auditory symptom severity was associated with a history of acoustic shock (Mann Whitney U = 344.0, p = .004) and with greater cognitive symptom burden (Spearman's {rho} = .416, p = .004), but not significantly with shift type (p = .177), years of work (p = .885), or daily and weekly working hours. Qualitative interviews described auditory strain that builds through the shift, disrupted sleep, informal coping, and the absence of employer guidance or symptom reporting pathways. Conclusion and Recommendations Self reported auditory symptoms were common in this preliminary sample of call center employees and were associated with acoustic shock exposure and cognitive symptom burden, but not significantly with shift pattern or length of service. Because the study was cross sectional, relied on self reports, and used a small volunteer sample (pilot study), the findings cannot establish causation or true prevalence. Recommended measures include acoustic shock limiters with incident reporting, audiometric screening that prioritizes at risk employees, safe volume education with regular breaks, and educational programs on auditory hazards and early warning signs to prevent actual auditory damage. Larger multi site studies with audiometric confirmation are also needed. Keywords: noise induced hearing loss; call center employees; occupational health; auditory dysfunction; tinnitus; acoustic shock; shift work; Egypt
